strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important problem: improving data efficiency and out-of-distribution generalization of implicit transfer operators (ITOs) for MD surrogate modeling, an active and impactful research area.

Clear, systematic ablation of different auxiliary conditioning signals (pLM sequence embeddings, structure embeddings, LLM-derived annotations), providing useful insight into what kinds of pretrained representations help (and, notably, what does not, e.g., the LLM annotations).

Strong empirical results: PLaTITO/PLaTITO-Big outperform the recent state-of-the-art Boltzmann Emulator BioEmu on equilibrium sampling metrics (MAE, RMSE, Coverage) for a battery of fast-folding proteins, while using roughly an order of magnitude less training data and compute — a compelling efficiency argument.

The evaluation goes beyond static equilibrium distributions to include dynamical/kinetic observables (mean first-passage times, non-Arrhenius temperature dependence of folding/unfolding rates) and a qualitative cryptic-pocket sampling case study, which strengthens the claim that the model learns physically meaningful dynamics rather than just matching marginal densities.
Reasonably transparent reporting of architecture, hyperparameters, training/sampling algorithms, and compute cost in the appendix, aiding reproducibility of the core recipe.

Honest limitations section explicitly acknowledging coarse-graining, lack of theoretical guarantees (detailed balance, Chapman-Kolmogorov), and limited generalization to complexes/extreme temperatures.
weaknesses: The primary benchmark (fast-folding proteins, Lindorff-Larsen et al.) is proprietary/available only upon request, which combined with mdCATH-based training limits full independent reproducibility of the headline comparisons for reviewers/readers without access.

Statistical rigor of the central comparisons is unclear: Table 1 reports mean±std across the 12 fast-folder systems, but it is not established whether differences between TITO/PLaTITO/PLaTITO+Struct are statistically significant given overlapping error bars (e.g., PLaTITO vs PLaTITO+Struct improvements are very small relative to reported spread).

The LLM-annotation component (Section 4.3-III) is a relatively weak and somewhat ad hoc contribution — it actually degrades performance, and the paper offers only speculative explanations ("prompting strategy or metadata insufficient") rather than a deeper investigation, making this part of the contribution feel underdeveloped relative to its prominence in the framing.

Comparisons to other closely related ITO-family baselines mentioned in Related Work (Timewarp, DeepJump, Boltzmann-prior ITO) are only discussed narratively and not benchmarked quantitatively alongside PLaTITO, so the improvement claim is validated mainly against BioEmu (a different model class) rather than against the most directly comparable transfer-operator methods.

The coarse-grained, Cα-only, non-equivariant modeling choice is a substantial simplification (acknowledged as a limitation) that likely limits applicability to tasks requiring side-chain detail (e.g., ligand binding, allostery), and the paper does not quantify how much accuracy is sacrificed relative to all-atom or equivariant alternatives.

Systematic underestimation of folding/unfolding timescales and failure to reproduce certain metastable basins/apo states in the cryptic pocket study indicate that the physical fidelity of the dynamics is still only qualitative, but the manuscript's abstract/conclusion language ("achieves state-of-the-art performance," "recovers non-Arrhenius rates") could be read as somewhat stronger than what the underlying evidence (small proprietary test set, qualitative kinetic trends, failure cases in Fig. 6) fully supports.
No explicit statement on code/model release, which affects reproducibility beyond the descriptive algorithm boxes provided.

strengths: The core idea—augmenting implicit transfer operator (ITO) training with pretrained protein sequence/structure embeddings—is a sensible, cheap-to-implement way to inject prior biological knowledge, and the ablation across TITO/PLaTITO/+Struct/+Struct+LLM/Big variants (Table 1, Section 5.1) gives a clear, controlled comparison of the different conditioning signals.

PLaTITO-Big is reported to match or outperform BioEmu on free-energy MAE/RMSE/Coverage for 12 out-of-distribution fast-folding proteins while using roughly 8x less training compute and data, which if correct is a practically meaningful efficiency result for the GenMD community (Table 1, Fig. 3).

The paper goes beyond stationary sampling to probe dynamical observables: MFPTs, non-Arrhenius temperature dependence of folding/unfolding rates, long roll-out trajectories showing repeated folding/unfolding, and cryptic pocket exploration, which is a more thorough evaluation than many comparable GenMD papers.

Reasonably detailed appendices (architecture, hyperparameters, sampling algorithms, LLM prompting protocol, per-system free-energy plots) support partial reproducibility, and the negative result for LLM-derived annotations is reported honestly rather than suppressed.
weaknesses: The headline comparison (PLaTITO-Big vs BioEmu) confounds multiple changes simultaneously: model capacity (3M→19M parameters) and pLM size (ESM-300M→ESM-6B) are scaled together, so it is unclear how much of the final gain is attributable to the proposed 'auxiliary information' idea versus simply using a larger backbone network; no controlled scaling ablation (e.g., 19M TITO without pLM, or 3M PLaTITO-Big-embedding) is provided to isolate this.

The comparison to BioEmu is not fully apples-to-apples: BioEmu solves a different task (direct i.i.d. equilibrium sampling without a Markovian rollout) and was trained with additional objectives (experimental ΔG, AFDB structures) for a different purpose (structure/ensemble generation broadly), so framing the GPU-hour and data comparisons as showing TITO is '10x more efficient' somewhat overstates the comparability of the two training regimes.

The coarse-grained Cα-only representation is a substantial limitation that the authors acknowledge but that significantly limits the scientific utility of the claimed 'equilibrium sampling' and 'kinetics' results, since side-chain packing is central to folding free energies and to the cryptic-pocket application the authors highlight as a future use case.

Per-system results in the appendix (Figs. 7-10) show that for several systems (e.g., NTL9, Homeodomain, Protein G, WW domain) the model's free-energy landscape only coarsely resembles the MD reference or misses metastable basins entirely; the aggregate MAE/RMSE/Coverage numbers in Table 1 mask this substantial per-system variability (note the very large standard deviations relative to the means), making the 'state-of-the-art' claim less convincing at the level of individual systems.

The claim that PLaTITO-Big 'recovers non-Arrhenius folding and unfolding rates' is only qualitative (visually non-linear Fig. 5) and not quantitatively validated against theory or with uncertainty propagation beyond MSM posterior variance; moreover the absolute MFPTs disagree with MD by roughly a factor of ~2-5x, which is explained away via the variational principle but without a quantitative correction or validation that this systematic bias doesn't also distort the qualitative Arrhenius deviation.

The LLM-derived annotation component (Section 4.3-III) is reported to decrease performance across all metrics (Table 1), yet it is still included as one of the three 'main' auxiliary signals and discussed extensively (Appendix C); this reads as a negative result inflated into a contribution, diluting the paper's focus rather than strengthening it.

The cryptic pocket results (Section 5.5, Fig. 6, Appendix D.4) are weak: the model fails to form clearly metastable basins in any of the four test systems and only marginally improves over BioEmu (succeeding in one of three BioEmu failure cases), which is a modest result presented with somewhat generous framing ('improves upon this').

Evaluation relies on a single curated dataset (mdCATH) for training and a single external benchmark (12 DESRES fast-folders, proprietary, available only upon request) for testing; broader generalization claims (e.g., to protein complexes, different force fields, or genuinely novel folds beyond small single-domain proteins) are not empirically supported and are explicitly deferred to future work.

The method is an incremental combination of existing components (TITO architecture from Diez et al., Proteina-style transformer, ESM/Proteina pretrained embeddings, flow matching), and the core architectural/methodological novelty beyond conditioning-signal engineering is limited.

strengths: The core idea—augmenting transferable implicit transfer operators (TITO) with pretrained protein sequence (pLM) and structure embeddings—is well-motivated and clearly described, building naturally on prior ITO/TITO literature.

The empirical scope is broad and relevant: equilibrium free-energy landscape reconstruction, long-timescale rollout dynamics (120 µs trajectories with repeated folding/unfolding), temperature-dependent kinetics (recovering non-Arrhenius behavior consistent with known folding physics), and cryptic pocket exploration.

PLaTITO-Big achieves lower MAE/RMSE and higher coverage than BioEmu on fast-folding proteins while using roughly an order of magnitude less training data and GPU-hours, which is a meaningful practical contribution for the field if the comparison is fair.

Reasonable reproducibility effort: architecture, training/sampling hyperparameters, and sampling/rollout algorithms are specified in detail in the appendix, and the dataset (mdCATH) and held-out benchmark (fast-folders) are clearly described with a sequence-similarity-based train/test split.

The ablation across TITO, PLaTITO, PLaTITO+Struct, and PLaTITO+Struct+LLM variants isolates the marginal contribution of each auxiliary signal, and the negative result for LLM annotations is reported honestly rather than omitted.

The limitations section is candid about the coarse-grained nature of the model and the lack of formal guarantees (detailed balance, Chapman-Kolmogorov consistency), which is appropriate scientific practice.
weaknesses: Potential data leakage concern: the pLM (ESM) embeddings are derived from models pretrained on enormous public sequence databases that likely include the fast-folding test sequences (or close homologs) seen during pLM pretraining; the 40% sequence-identity train/test filter only controls for overlap with the TITO training set, not for information the pretrained pLM/structure models may have memorized about these specific proteins' stability or folding behavior, which could inflate the apparent benefit of PLaTITO on this particular benchmark.

Several headline comparisons have overlapping error bars (e.g., TITO MAE 1.068±0.272 vs PLaTITO 0.949±0.269), and no significance testing (e.g., paired tests across systems) is reported, making it hard to assess whether differences between variants are statistically robust rather than noise, especially for the smaller/modest gains from structure embeddings.

The LLM-annotation conditioning actually degrades performance, but the paper offers only a brief, somewhat speculative explanation (prompting/metadata insufficiency) without further diagnostic analysis (e.g., does performance degrade uniformly or only on systems flagged as low-confidence/unsuitable?), limiting the interpretability of this negative result.

Comparisons are made against a single external baseline (BioEmu); other relevant transfer-operator baselines explicitly discussed in Related Work (e.g., DeepJump, Timewarp, Boltzmann-prior ITO) are not benchmarked head-to-head on the same equilibrium/kinetics tasks, which would strengthen claims of state-of-the-art performance.

The systematic underestimation of folding/unfolding timescales (and failure to form clearly metastable apo/holo basins in cryptic pocket experiments) is acknowledged but not quantitatively characterized or corrected for, leaving open how reliable the kinetic predictions are in absolute terms versus just qualitative trend recovery.

The coarse-grained Cα-only representation, while reasonable for scaling, is a substantial limitation for several of the paper's own motivating use-cases (e.g., cryptic pocket/ligand-relevant conformational sampling), and the paper does not provide a roadmap or quantitative estimate of how much this limits accuracy versus an all-atom counterpart.

Training compute/steps differ slightly across model variants (e.g., different number of training steps, batch sizes, and architecture widths for PLaTITO-Big vs. smaller variants in Table 2), which, combined with matched GPU-hours but different per-step costs, makes the scaling comparisons only approximately controlled rather than a clean ablation of a single factor.

strengths: Strong empirical results: PLaTITO-19M achieves state-of-the-art equilibrium sampling metrics (MAE, RMSE, Coverage) on fast-folding proteins while using ~8x less training compute (1100 vs 9216 GPU hours) and much less data than the BioEmu baseline, a compelling data-efficiency claim.

Extensive and well-designed ablations: systematic comparison of pLM family/size (ESMC 300M/600M/6B, ESM2), model capacity scaling (1M-100M params), and auxiliary conditioning signals (structure embeddings, LLM annotations), which clarify which components actually help and by how much.

Comparisons against multiple relevant baselines (BioEmu, ConfDiff, Str2Str, a matched Boltzmann-Emulator control 'Emu') isolate the contribution of exploiting MD auto-correlation structure (ITO framework) versus auxiliary embeddings versus raw compute/data scale.

Goes beyond static equilibrium sampling to evaluate dynamical observables (folding/unfolding MFPTs, non-Arrhenius temperature dependence, long 120 µs rollout trajectories, cryptic pocket exploration), providing a richer and more convincing validation of the learned transition operator than distribution matching alone.
Reasonably thorough reproducibility support: detailed appendices with architecture, hyperparameters, training/sampling algorithms, and metric definitions.

Honest limitations section (coarse-graining, lack of formal guarantees such as detailed balance/Chapman-Kolmogorov, limited generalization outside trained temperature/chemical range) and honest reporting of negative/mixed results (LLM annotations hurt performance, failures in 2/4 cryptic pocket systems).
weaknesses: The core architecture is largely a recombination of existing components (Proteina-based transformer backbone, ESM/pLM embeddings, rectified flow matching, ITO framework from Schreiner et al. and Diez et al.), so the technical novelty is primarily in the specific combination and empirical study rather than a fundamentally new method.

The primary evaluation benchmark (Lindorff-Larsen fast-folding trajectories) is proprietary and 'available upon request,' which limits independent reproducibility of the main results despite code availability for the model itself.

Differences between several model variants in Table 1 (e.g., TITO vs TITO+Struct, PLaTITO vs PLaTITO+Struct) are numerically small relative to reported standard deviations, and no formal statistical significance testing is provided, making some comparative claims (e.g., structure embeddings provide 'complementary' benefit) somewhat weakly supported.

The negative result for LLM-derived annotations is not thoroughly investigated; the paper offers only speculative explanations (prompting strategy or metadata insufficiency) without deeper analysis or ablation of prompt design, which leaves this contribution underexplored.

Systematic underestimation of folding/unfolding timescales relative to MD reference (Figure 5, Section 5.3) is acknowledged but not deeply analyzed; the explanation via the variational principle is plausible but not rigorously validated for this specific coarse-grained non-equivariant setting.

The model inherits significant limitations from the ITO framework (no guarantees of detailed balance, Chapman-Kolmogorov consistency, or unbiased equilibrium sampling), and the coarse-grained (Cα-only) representation precludes analysis of side-chain-dependent phenomena, restricting applicability to drug-discovery relevant tasks like precise binding-pocket geometry.

Cryptic pocket results, while promising, still show failures in half the tested systems (2 of 4) and do not yet reach clearly metastable free-energy basins, indicating the practical utility for this application remains limited at current scale.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: improving data efficiency and out-of-distribution generalization of generative MD surrogates (implicit transfer operators), which is a genuine bottleneck for this class of methods.

Extensive ablations are provided (Appendix D.3-D.5): varying pLM family/size, model capacity (1M-100M params), and comparisons against several strong baselines (BioEmu, ConfDiff, Str2Str, a custom 'Emu' Boltzmann-emulator control). This level of ablation is commendable and helps isolate the source of gains.

The headline comparison against BioEmu is compelling on its face: PLaTITO-19M reports better MAE/RMSE/Coverage while using roughly an order of magnitude less training data and GPU-hours, which, if robust, would be a meaningful practical contribution.

The temperature-conditioned kinetics analysis (non-Arrhenius folding/unfolding rates, Figure 5) is a nice qualitative sanity check that goes beyond simple equilibrium-distribution matching and lends some physical credibility to the learned dynamics.

The limitations section is honest and appropriately scoped, acknowledging the coarse-grained nature of the model and the lack of formal guarantees (detailed balance, Chapman-Kolmogorov, etc.) inherited from the ITO framework.
The cryptic-pocket case study provides a nuanced, non-cherry-picked discussion of partial successes and failure modes rather than simply claiming victory.
weaknesses: Statistical significance of the central claim is weak: in Table 1, the reported standard deviations for MAE/RMSE/Coverage largely overlap between TITO, PLaTITO, and PLaTITO+Struct (e.g., PLaTITO 0.949±0.269 vs. TITO 1.068±0.272; PLaTITO vs. PLaTITO+Struct differ by <0.02 with std >0.3). No significance testing (e.g., paired tests across the 11 systems) is reported, so it is unclear whether the 'consistent improvement' from pLM embeddings is more than noise given the small number of evaluation systems (11-12 fast-folders).

The LLM-annotation contribution (one of three proposed auxiliary signals and part of 'Contribution 2') actually degrades performance (PLaTITO+Struct+LLM underperforms PLaTITO+Struct and is close to or worse than base TITO), undermining the generality of the auxiliary-conditioning narrative and leaving an unresolved negative result presented somewhat passively.

Evaluation is restricted to a coarse-grained Cα-only representation and a narrow benchmark (12 small fast-folding proteins, typically <80 residues, plus 4 cryptic-pocket systems), which limits the strength of 'state-of-the-art' and 'generalization' claims; the Impact Statement's suggestion of near-term applicability to drug discovery seems overstated relative to what coarse-grained, backbone-only sampling can actually deliver.

The architecture is explicitly non-equivariant, which is an unusual choice for 3D molecular coordinates given that most competing methods (BioEmu, ConfDiff, Timewarp, TITO's predecessor) use equivariant or augmentation-based designs; no ablation isolates how much of the claimed data efficiency comes from pLM conditioning versus architectural or training differences relative to the cited TITO baseline (Diez et al.) itself.

Train/test leakage control uses only 40% sequence identity filtering; this does not rule out structural/fold-level homology or functional similarity that could inflate apparent generalization, which is particularly relevant for small, well-studied fast-folders that may be structurally similar to common folds in mdCATH.

Qualitative inspection of the appendix free-energy landscapes shows that several systems (e.g., Trp-cage, parts of A3D, Homeodomain) are still visibly quite different from the MD reference despite favorable aggregate metrics, suggesting the 2D TICA-binned MAE/RMSE/Coverage metrics may not fully capture distributional fidelity; the authors themselves note Coverage can be a misleading metric (as demonstrated by Str2Str's high Coverage but poor landscapes), raising concern about over-reliance on these metrics elsewhere in the paper.
The provided code link is a placeholder ('https://github.com/') rather than a working repository, which is a reproducibility concern at submission time.

The method systematically underestimates folding/unfolding timescales and fails to form metastable basins in some apo/holo cryptic-pocket cases, and the authors' own discussion suggests these are not minor artifacts but persistent limitations across several benchmarks, somewhat tempering the significance of the 'state-of-the-art' framing.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical study with systematic ablations isolating the effect of sequence embeddings (pLM), structure embeddings, and LLM-derived annotations on a common TITO backbone, trained under matched data and compute budgets.

Strong headline result: PLaTITO-19M outperforms BioEmu across all reported equilibrium sampling metrics (MAE, RMSE, Coverage) on out-of-distribution fast-folding proteins while using roughly an order of magnitude less training data and GPU compute, which is a practically meaningful efficiency gain if it holds up.

Goes beyond static equilibrium sampling to probe dynamical/kinetic properties: recovers non-Arrhenius temperature-dependent folding/unfolding rates and explores cryptic pocket conformations, adding qualitative physical plausibility checks beyond simple distributional matching.
Thorough scaling studies (pLM family/size ablation, model capacity ablation from 1M-100M parameters) that build a coherent narrative about complementary scaling of embeddings and model capacity.

Extensive appendices with algorithms (training/sampling pseudocode), hyperparameters, per-system free-energy landscapes, additional baselines (ConfDiff, Str2Str), and inference-speed benchmarking, supporting reproducibility and giving confidence the results are not cherry-picked to a few systems.
Honest limitations section acknowledging coarse-graining, lack of formal guarantees (detailed balance, Chapman-Kolmogorov), and likely limited generalization across chemical space/temperature.
weaknesses: The comparison against BioEmu as evidence of data/compute efficiency is confounded: BioEmu is trained on a different architecture, objective (direct Boltzmann sampling vs. transfer-operator rollout) and additional data sources (AFDB structures, experimental ΔG), making the 10x compute/data claim more of an existence proof than a controlled comparison.

The LLM-derived annotation component (PLaTITO+Struct+LLM) actually degrades performance, and the paper offers only a speculative explanation (poor prompting or insufficient metadata) without deeper diagnostic analysis of why this heuristic failed, weakening this particular contribution.

The coarse-grained Cα-only representation limits the physical relevance of the model for stated downstream applications (cryptic pocket/ligand binding, drug discovery), since side-chain motions are ignored; the cryptic-pocket results themselves show the model fails to form clear metastable basins in several cases.

Predicted folding/unfolding timescales are systematically faster than MD reference (underestimated), and while attributed to a known variational bias, this is a non-trivial quantitative discrepancy that is not further corrected or bounded.

Evaluation metrics rely on 2D TICA projections and coarse histogram binning (MAE/RMSE/Coverage), which may not fully capture higher-dimensional conformational accuracy; no all-atom or side-chain-level validation is possible given the CG design.

Reliance on proprietary fast-folding MD trajectories (available only upon request) and reliance on a commercial LLM (DeepSeek) for annotation generation introduce reproducibility friction beyond the released code.

Performance peaks at 36M parameters and degrades at 100M, with limited investigation into whether this is a data-limited scaling bottleneck or an architectural/training issue, leaving the scaling story somewhat incomplete.
